title: Protecting routes in React
intro: React can protect the user experience, but it cannot be the final security boundary because the API must enforce authorization. In this lesson, you will build a small authentication context, protect routes and UI based on the current user, and handle expired authentication cleanly.
body:
## The frontend is not the security boundary A React application can make authenticated parts of your application feel secure, but it cannot actually enforce access to your data. ~~~callout warn Hiding a button is not security Route guards and role-based UI only improve the experience. Anyone can open DevTools and call `DELETE /api/users/7` directly — the backend must reject it with **403** on its own. ~~~ The browser is controlled by the user. They can modify JavaScript, call your API directly, change requests in developer tools, or write their own client. That means your React application should handle authentication state and user experience, while the Spring Boot API remains responsible for real security. For example, React can decide whether to display an Admin link: ~~~tsx {user?.role === "ADMIN" && Admin} ~~~ That is good UX. It prevents ordinary users from seeing a navigation option they cannot use. It is not authorization. The backend must still reject an unauthorized request to an admin endpoint. A useful rule is: > The frontend controls what the user sees. The backend controls what the user is allowed to do. ## Keeping authentication state with AuthContext React provides **Context**, a mechanism for making a value available to components without passing it through every intermediate component as a prop. For authentication, an `AuthContext` can hold the current user and operations such as login and logout. A simple context might look like this: ~~~tsx const AuthContext = React.createContext(null); ~~~ The application then uses an `AuthProvider` component to hold the actual state: ~~~tsx function AuthProvider({ children }) { const [user, setUser] = React.useState(null); function login(name, role) { setUser({ name, role }); } function logout() { setUser(null); } return ( {children} ); } ~~~ A component can retrieve the context with `useContext`: ~~~tsx const auth = React.useContext(AuthContext); ~~~ Now the component can access the current user and call `login` or `logout` without receiving those values through several layers of props. In a real application, the context might contain more information, such as whether authentication is still being checked, the user's permissions, or a function for refreshing authentication. ## Protecting routes A typical React application uses React Router to map URLs to components. You can place a protection component around routes that require authentication. ~~~diagram {"type": "flow", "title": "What decides", "nodes": [{"id": "nav", "label": "Navigate to /admin", "kind": "user"}, {"id": "g", "label": "", "kind": "code", "highlight": true}, {"id": "load", "label": "Checking session…", "sub": "render nothing yet"}, {"id": "login", "label": "", "sub": "remember where they came from"}, {"id": "deny", "label": "403 page"}, {"id": "page", "label": "Admin page", "kind": "client", "highlight": true}], "edges": [{"from": "nav", "to": "g"}, {"from": "g", "to": "load", "label": "loading", "dashed": true}, {"from": "g", "to": "login", "label": "no user"}, {"from": "g", "to": "deny", "label": "wrong role"}, {"from": "g", "to": "page", "label": "ok"}]} ~~~ Conceptually: ~~~tsx } /> ~~~ A `ProtectedRoute` checks the current authentication state. If the user is logged in, it renders the requested page. If not, it redirects to `/login`. The important part is remembering where the user wanted to go. Imagine someone opens: ~~~text /tasks/123 ~~~ but they are not logged in. The application can redirect them to: ~~~text /login?returnTo=/tasks/123 ~~~ After a successful login, the application can send them back to `/tasks/123` instead of always sending them to the dashboard. React Router provides navigation and location APIs that make this pattern straightforward. The exact implementation depends on the router version used by the project. ## Role-based UI Authentication alone does not tell you what a user can see. Our task manager might have two roles: ~~~text USER ADMIN ~~~ You can use the authenticated user's role to adjust navigation and interface elements: ~~~tsx function Navigation() { const { user } = React.useContext(AuthContext); return (
Tasks {user?.role === "ADMIN" && Admin}
); } ~~~ This keeps the interface clean. A normal user does not need to see controls that are irrelevant to them. But remember that this is still a frontend convenience. If `/api/admin/users` requires administrator access, the backend must check the authenticated user's role on that request. The same principle applies to buttons: ~~~tsx {user?.role === "ADMIN" && ( )} ~~~ The backend must independently verify the permission when the delete operation is requested. ## Sending the token with fetch Once a user is authenticated, the frontend needs to authenticate API requests. For a bearer-token API, the request commonly includes an `Authorization` header: ~~~ts const response = await fetch("/api/tasks", { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` } }); ~~~ `Bearer` tells the server that the value is a bearer credential. Whoever possesses a valid bearer token can generally use it until it expires or is otherwise invalidated, so protecting these credentials matters. In a real application, you will usually avoid repeating this code manually in every component. A small API client function can attach the access token consistently: ~~~ts async function apiFetch(url, token) { return fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } }); } ~~~ As your application grows, you can build a more complete API layer that handles JSON, errors, authentication, and common request options in one place. ## Handling 401 responses Authentication can expire while the user is using your application. ~~~diagram {"type": "sequence", "title": "An expired token", "actors": ["Page", "apiClient", "API"], "steps": [{"from": "Page", "to": "apiClient", "label": "getTickets()"}, {"from": "apiClient", "to": "API", "label": "GET /api/tickets + Bearer"}, {"from": "API", "to": "apiClient", "label": "401", "dashed": true}, {"note": "clear token, logout()", "over": "apiClient"}, {"from": "apiClient", "to": "Page", "label": "redirect to /login?next=/tickets", "dashed": true}]} ~~~ For example, a user might leave the task manager open for an hour. Their access token expires, and the next API request returns `401 Unauthorized`. The frontend should respond to that state rather than pretending the user is still authenticated. A simple pattern is: ~~~ts const response = await fetch("/api/tasks", options); if (response.status === 401) { logout(); // navigate to /login } ~~~ You can also centralize this behaviour in an API client. Then every request gets consistent handling. A `401` means authentication is missing or no longer valid. A `403` is different: the server knows who the user is, but that user is not allowed to perform the requested operation. For example: ~~~text Expired access token -> 401 -> log in again Authenticated USER accessing ADMIN operation -> 403 -> show access denied ~~~ Do not automatically treat every `403` as a logout. The user may be correctly authenticated but simply lack permission. ## Where should the token live? Browser token storage is an important security design decision. One approach is to keep a short-lived access token in JavaScript memory. The advantage is that it is not persisted in browser storage. The disadvantage is that the token disappears when the page is fully reloaded. A common architecture is to combine this with a refresh token held in an `HttpOnly` cookie. An `HttpOnly` cookie cannot normally be read by JavaScript. This makes it harder for injected JavaScript to directly steal the refresh credential. The basic flow can look like this: ~~~text Login ↓ short-lived access token in memory + refresh token in HttpOnly cookie ↓ API requests use access token ↓ access token expires ↓ refresh request automatically uses cookie ↓ new access token returned ~~~ This architecture still requires careful CSRF protection because cookies are automatically sent by the browser in appropriate requests. Avoid using `localStorage` for long-lived authentication tokens as a default strategy. JavaScript can read `localStorage`, so an XSS vulnerability could potentially expose a token stored there. There is no single storage mechanism that makes a frontend automatically secure. Token lifetime, XSS protection, cookie configuration, CSRF protection, refresh-token rotation, and backend authorization all matter. ## Avoiding protected-content flashes There is a subtle UI problem when authentication must be checked asynchronously. Suppose the application starts with: ~~~ts const [user, setUser] = React.useState(null); ~~~ If the application immediately renders the login page or a denied message, it may briefly show the wrong screen while it checks whether a valid session or refresh credential exists. This is often called an **auth flash**: protected or incorrect content briefly appears before the application knows the real authentication state. A better approach is to track a separate loading state: ~~~tsx const [user, setUser] = React.useState(null); const [checkingAuth, setCheckingAuth] = React.useState(true); if (checkingAuth) { return

Checking your session...

; } ~~~ Once the initial authentication check finishes, the application can decide whether to render protected content or redirect to login. This distinction is important: ~~~text user === null could mean: - definitely logged out - authentication has not been checked yet ~~~ Using an explicit loading state lets the application distinguish those situations. ## A practical protected-route structure Putting the ideas together, a real task manager might have a structure similar to: ~~~text App └── AuthProvider ├── Public routes │ └── Login └── Protected routes ├── Dashboard ├── Tasks └── Admin ~~~ The authentication provider owns the current authentication state. The route protection component decides whether a user may enter a protected route. Individual UI components can use the context to display appropriate controls. The API client attaches the access token and handles expired authentication. The Spring Boot backend remains the actual security boundary. ## Common mistakes ### Treating protected React routes as backend security A user can bypass your React router completely and call the API directly. Always enforce authentication and authorization in Spring Security and your backend application logic. ### Logging out on every error Only authentication failures such as `401` should normally trigger an authentication recovery flow. A `403` means the user is authenticated but forbidden from performing the operation. ### Storing long-lived tokens in localStorage JavaScript can read `localStorage`. An XSS vulnerability could therefore expose credentials stored there. Prefer short-lived tokens in memory with a carefully designed refresh mechanism when appropriate. ### Showing protected content while authentication is loading If the application has not finished checking authentication, do not immediately assume that the user is logged out. Use an explicit loading state to avoid incorrect content flashes. ### Hiding only some admin controls Frontend role checks should be consistent, but they are still only UX. Every sensitive backend operation must independently enforce authorization. ## Putting it together The frontend authentication flow can now be understood as a sequence: ~~~text Application starts ↓ Check existing authentication ↓ Show loading state while checking ↓ Authenticated? ── no ──> /login │ yes ↓ Store current user in AuthContext ↓ Render protected routes and role-specific UI ↓ Attach access token to API requests ↓ 401? ── yes ──> refresh or logout/login ↓ Backend performs the real authorization check ~~~ The key distinction remains the same throughout the application: React manages the user's experience around authentication, while Spring Boot decides whether an operation is actually allowed. This separation makes the frontend easier to reason about and prevents a common security mistake: assuming that something is secure merely because the user interface does not expose it.
takeaways: React can improve authentication UX, but the backend must enforce every real security rule.
AuthContext is a convenient place to keep the current user and login/logout operations available to the component tree.
Protected routes can redirect unauthenticated users and remember the destination they originally requested.
Handle 401 responses as authentication failures, while treating 403 responses as authenticated-but-forbidden requests.
Use an explicit authentication-loading state so protected content does not flash before the initial auth check finishes.

quiz.question: What is the primary security role of a React protected route?
options: It prevents the backend from receiving unauthorized HTTP requests
It provides a better user experience by controlling which UI and routes are shown
It encrypts all API responses
It replaces Spring Security
quiz.explanation: React route protection is primarily a user-experience mechanism. The backend must still enforce authentication and authorization on API requests.

quiz.question: What is a useful purpose of AuthContext?
options: To store PostgreSQL tables in React
To compile Spring Boot controllers
To make authentication state and operations such as login/logout available to components
To automatically verify JWT signatures
quiz.explanation: AuthContext can expose the current user and authentication operations throughout the React component tree without passing them through every component as props.

quiz.question: What should a frontend generally do when a protected API request receives HTTP 401?
options: Treat the user as authenticated forever
Ignore the response and display the old data
Automatically grant the user ADMIN privileges
Attempt the appropriate authentication recovery or log the user out and require login
quiz.explanation: A 401 indicates that authentication is missing or no longer valid. Depending on the architecture, the application can refresh authentication or log the user out and send them to login.

quiz.question: Why should long-lived authentication tokens generally not be stored in localStorage?
options: JavaScript can read localStorage, so an XSS vulnerability could expose the token
React cannot access localStorage
Browsers delete localStorage every minute
Spring Security rejects tokens stored in localStorage
quiz.explanation: localStorage is accessible to JavaScript running on the page. If malicious JavaScript executes because of an XSS vulnerability, it may be able to read a token stored there.

quiz.question: Why should an application have an explicit authentication-loading state?
options: To make passwords easier to guess
To avoid showing the wrong protected or login content before authentication has been checked
To disable backend authorization
To make every request return 403
quiz.explanation: Authentication may need to be checked asynchronously. A loading state prevents the UI from incorrectly assuming that a user is logged out before that check finishes.

exercise.title: Build a protected React UI
exercise.task:
Build a small authentication system using React Context and state. Do not use a router library for this exercise. Create `AuthContext` with `React.createContext`, and create an `AuthProvider` that stores `user`, initially `null`, where a logged-in user has `{ name, role }`. The provider must expose `login(name, role)` and `logout()`. Create `RequireAuth({ role, children })`. It should render its `children` when a user is logged in and, when a `role` is provided, only when the user has that role. If there is no logged-in user, render a `

` with `data-testid="denied"` containing exactly `Please log in`. If the user is logged in but does not have the required role, render the same element containing exactly `Not allowed`. `App` must render inside `AuthProvider` and contain buttons named `Log in as user`, `Log in as admin`, and `Log out`. The first login button must call `login("Anna", "USER")`; the second must call `login("Bence", "ADMIN")`. Add a `RequireAuth` section containing `

Dashboard

` and another `RequireAuth` with `role="ADMIN"` containing `

Admin

`. The tests will click the buttons and check which headings and messages are visible. This exercise models frontend authentication state only; the real API must still enforce authentication and authorization on the backend.
exercise.hint: Keep the current user in AuthProvider with useState and expose it through the context. RequireAuth can read that context with useContext, first checking for no user and then checking the requested role. App should also read login and logout from the same context.

tests.name: It asks logged-out users to log in
tests.code: const denied = document.querySelectorAll('[data-testid="denied"]'); const headings = [...document.querySelectorAll("h2")]; return denied.length === 2 && [...denied].every(el => el.textContent === "Please log in") && headings.length === 0;

tests.name: A normal user can see the dashboard
tests.code: const button = [...document.querySelectorAll("button")].find(el => el.textContent === "Log in as user"); if (!button) throw new Error("User login button not found"); await click(button); const headings = [...document.querySelectorAll("h2")].map(el => el.textContent); const denied = [...document.querySelectorAll('[data-testid="denied"]')].map(el => el.textContent); return headings.includes("Dashboard") && !headings.includes("Admin") && denied.length === 1 && denied[0] === "Not allowed";

tests.name: An admin can see both sections
tests.code: const button = [...document.querySelectorAll("button")].find(el => el.textContent === "Log in as admin"); if (!button) throw new Error("Admin login button not found"); await click(button); const headings = [...document.querySelectorAll("h2")].map(el => el.textContent); const denied = document.querySelector('[data-testid="denied"]'); return headings.includes("Dashboard") && headings.includes("Admin") && !denied;

tests.name: Logging out hides protected sections
tests.code: const admin = [...document.querySelectorAll("button")].find(el => el.textContent === "Log in as admin"); if (!admin) throw new Error("Admin login button not found"); await click(admin); const logout = [...document.querySelectorAll("button")].find(el => el.textContent === "Log out"); if (!logout) throw new Error("Logout button not found"); await click(logout); const headings = document.querySelectorAll("h2"); const denied = [...document.querySelectorAll('[data-testid="denied"]')].map(el => el.textContent); return headings.length === 0 && denied.length === 2 && denied.every(text => text === "Please log in");

tests.name: A normal user cannot access the admin section
tests.code: const button = [...document.querySelectorAll("button")].find(el => el.textContent === "Log in as user"); if (!button) throw new Error("User login button not found"); await click(button); const admin = [...document.querySelectorAll("h2")].find(el => el.textContent === "Admin"); const denied = document.querySelector('[data-testid="denied"]'); return !admin && denied && denied.textContent === "Not allowed";

tests.name: An admin can access the admin section
tests.code: const button = [...document.querySelectorAll("button")].find(el => el.textContent === "Log in as admin"); if (!button) throw new Error("Admin login button not found"); await click(button); const admin = [...document.querySelectorAll("h2")].find(el => el.textContent === "Admin"); return !!admin;
